species.label: Syn3A
species.plain: A bacterium with a designed, minimised genome of 452 protein-coding genes, proposed as the first whole-cell validation organism for Cells; the units of the law inventory are machines of animal cells, and it has none of them.

method: The organism's proteins are the 455 protein products of one frozen genome annotation, GenBank CP016816.2 (annotation of 12 April 2018): 452 kept from Mycoplasma mycoides and 3 added for genetic manipulation. UniProtKB holds no entry of the organism; UniProt's archive (UniParc) holds exactly these 455 sequences, with the family signatures on each.
Licences were read before anything was copied; each is stated in sources, and what was read but not copied is in not_copied.
Each unit's family was taken from its own human candidates, by the same InterPro signatures that the planarian atlas asks. The build checks that the candidates carry them.
Each signature was looked for on all 455 sequences. None was found, for any unit.
A control for every zero: the same signature was asked of the UniProtKB entries of all mollicutes, the class of bacteria the organism was made from; each unit's note gives what came back.

Eight further signatures, of the ion channels a bacterium could have (potassium, chloride, magnesium, water and membrane-stretch channels), were looked for as well, and none was found, although each is carried by UniProtKB entries of other mollicutes.

Under extra are nine of the organism's own membrane machines that bear on what the atlas draws and match no unit. Five are named for this organism in Breuer and others 2019, whose saved text the build checks; four are listed by the signature on their sequence. All are assigned by annotation, not measured in this strain.
No similarity search was run, and nothing is called an ortholog.

not_copied: No sequence is copied: they stay with the downloads, outside the repository. Nothing is taken from the 2022 whole-cell paper, which is under a non-commercial licence (CC BY-NC-ND), or from the 2021 paper on the genes needed for division, which states no open licence: the species file names both as places to read, and what it says of energy and of division rests on the 2019 paper and on an open review. The 2026 whole-cell paper and the archive of its model were not read for this file, and the instrument files of the 2019 proteomics (PXD008159) were not downloaded.

U01.note: None of the 455 protein products of its genome carries the signature of voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunits and sodium channel beta subunits (IPR001696, IPR027098, IPR000920). No UniProtKB entry of any mollicute, the class of bacteria it was made from, carries them either. The unit's human candidates carry them, so the search finds the family where it exists. No ion channel of any family searched was found in this organism: its ions cross the membrane through transporters and pumps.

extra.name: ATP synthase, F1 alpha subunit
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0792, product "F0F1 ATP synthase subunit alpha" in the genome record. Its sequence carries IPR000194 (ATPase, F1/V1/A1 complex, alpha/beta subunit, nucleotide-binding domain) in UniProt's archive. A candidate by annotation, not a measured function in this strain.
extra.why: Part of the cell's F-type ATP synthase, which sits in its one membrane; four of its eight subunits are listed here. The 2019 reconstruction of the cell's metabolism has this machine push protons out of the cell; that is a model's reading, not a measurement in this strain. The law inventory has no F-type ATPase.

extra.name: ATP synthase, F1 beta subunit
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0790, product "F0F1 ATP synthase subunit beta" in the genome record. Its sequence carries IPR000194 (ATPase, F1/V1/A1 complex, alpha/beta subunit, nucleotide-binding domain) in UniProt's archive. A candidate by annotation, not a measured function in this strain.
extra.why: The other subunit of the ATP synthase's catalytic head. The 2019 paper found the genes of this machine essential.

extra.name: ATP synthase, F0 c subunit
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0795, product "F0F1 ATP synthase subunit C" in the genome record. Its sequence carries IPR000454 (ATP synthase, F0 complex, subunit C) in UniProt's archive. A candidate by annotation, not a measured function in this strain.
extra.why: The ring of the ATP synthase that carries protons across the membrane.

extra.name: ATP synthase, F0 a subunit
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0796, product "F0F1 ATP synthase subunit A" in the genome record. Its sequence carries IPR000568 (ATP synthase, F0 complex, subunit A) in UniProt's archive. A candidate by annotation, not a measured function in this strain.
extra.why: The membrane subunit of the ATP synthase beside the ring, where protons enter and leave.

extra.name: P-type ATPase MgtA
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0787, product "Magnesium-translocating P-type ATPase" in the genome record. Breuer and others 2019 name it: the annotation lists it as an importer of magnesium. The role is assigned from its sequence and from related mycoplasmas, not measured in this strain.

citation.text: Breuer and others (2019) Essential metabolism for a minimal cell. eLife 8:e36842.

extra.why: A pump of the same superfamily as the sodium-potassium and calcium pumps of animal cells, of another branch: its annotation calls it magnesium-translocating.

extra.name: P-type ATPase annotated as CorA
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0879, product "Magnesium transporter" in the genome record. Breuer and others 2019 name it: a putative magnesium importer that could carry calcium as well; the paper's reconstruction uses it as the calcium importer. The role is assigned from its sequence and from related mycoplasmas, not measured in this strain.

citation.text: Breuer and others (2019) Essential metabolism for a minimal cell. eLife 8:e36842.

extra.why: Its annotation calls it a magnesium transporter and names it corA, but its signatures are those of a cation-transporting P-type ATPase and not of the CorA channel family. It is the nearest thing this organism has to a calcium pump.

extra.name: Potassium uptake protein KtrB-like
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0685, product "Sodium transporter" in the genome record. Breuer and others 2019 name it: with locus 0686, the KtrAB potassium import system; the paper's reconstruction gives it an ATP-consuming exchange of potassium for sodium. The role is assigned from its sequence and from related mycoplasmas, not measured in this strain.

citation.text: Breuer and others (2019) Essential metabolism for a minimal cell. eLife 8:e36842.

extra.why: The membrane part of the cell's potassium uptake system. This is how the organism takes up potassium without a sodium-potassium pump or a potassium channel. Its annotation calls it a sodium transporter (natA).

extra.name: Potassium uptake protein KtrA-like
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0686, product "Potassium transporter" in the genome record. Breuer and others 2019 name it: with locus 0685, the KtrAB potassium import system. The role is assigned from its sequence and from related mycoplasmas, not measured in this strain.

citation.text: Breuer and others (2019) Essential metabolism for a minimal cell. eLife 8:e36842.

extra.why: The cytoplasmic partner of the potassium uptake system, annotated trkA.

extra.name: Glucose transporter PtsG
extra.evidence_note: Locus JCVISYN3A_0779, product "PTS sugar transporter" in the genome record. Breuer and others 2019 name it: part of the glucose phosphotransferase system, the only annotated sugar importer. The role is assigned from its sequence and from related mycoplasmas, not measured in this strain.

citation.text: Breuer and others (2019) Essential metabolism for a minimal cell. eLife 8:e36842.

extra.why: The membrane part of the system that brings in glucose, the cell's fuel. Its ATP comes from fermenting that sugar.
